newsitem.title: GREECE: GREECE TO EXAMINE BANNING GENE-TOMATOES RESEARCH.
newsitem.headline: GREECE TO EXAMINE BANNING GENE-TOMATOES RESEARCH.

text.p: Greece said it will consider scrapping research on genetically-altered tomatoes after protests by Greenpeace activists on Tuesday.
Greece, which opposes the production, import and use of genetically engineered food, gave a permit in March to a private company to experiment with tomatoes to extend their ripening time.
Extending their ripening time would mean that tomatoes would have a longer shelf-life in stores.

Greenpeace activists dressed as tomatoes posted a sign outside the Environment Ministry reading "Ministry of Transmutations and Genetic Dangers" before meeting Deputy Environment Minister Theodoros Koliopanos.

"The deputy minister said no new permits for genetically altered foods will be granted and that it will examine the option of cancelling a permit granted to the Zeneca company for genetically altered tomatoes," Greenpeace activist Nikos Charalambidis told Reuters.
Ministry officials said the minister was concerned after his meeting with Greenpeace officials and was prepared to cancel the research permit if presented with new evidence that it was dangerous.
"The minister opposes genetically-engineered food. He signed this permit only for research but he is prepared to recall it," one ministry official said.
Greenpeace and other enviromental groups have launched an international campaign against gene-altered foods, such as soybeans and corn, saying they may have unknown health risks.
"We are used to protests about experiments on animals. It's time we protest about experiments on us," Charalambidis said.
Greek ministry officials said they considered research into the gene-altered tomatoes safe because it was kept within the controlled environment of a greenhouse.
But Greenpeace said there was no way to prevent the results of genetic testing in a greenhouse from reaching the environment because insects and pollen could not be stopped from intefering.
It asked the minister to ban the release of genetically engineeted organisms to the environment and to work with other European Union countries to adopt strict measures against them.
"Greenpeace also asks consumers to pressure companies, supermarket chains and politicians to stop supplying markets with genetically engineered products," Charalambidis said.
More than a million Austrians have signed a petition calling for a ban on genetically modified foods, forcing a parliamentary debate on the issue this month.
